column2: The enemy, whether boy, non-boy or old man, who would always strike a careless man—another, in time, would take away his root; the knower of time is the best of kings.
He would take away fame, obstruct his dharma, and destroy his long-held strength in wealth; whether the enemy is hateful, weak or strong, the self-controlled should never slight a foe.
The decline of the enemy, one's own accumulation and protection—both aims together serve dharma and desire; hence the wise man should arrange the rest; therefore a king should rely on the wise.
Blazing intellect destroys the strong; strength grows when guarded by intellect; the enemy, growing, sinks by intellect; praised is the deed that follows intellect.
The steadfast, desiring all desires, wading with little strength, of slight body, as he wishes for himself with his wealth, fills a vessel of the good not little.
Therefore a king, once seized by enemies, should take up from all sides the root of fortune; even long oppressed, he should be glorious, like the fall of lightning.
Knowledge, austerity or vast wealth—all this is possible by resolve; Brahman, which dwells in embodied beings, therefore know resolve to be abundant.
Where the wise and the high-minded dwell, where Shakra, Vishnu and Sarasvati and all beings ever abide—therefore the learned man should not despise the body.

One should always slay the greedy by gifts; the greedy never reaches satisfaction with another's wealth; every greedy man works for the enjoyment of qualities; he who is without wealth gives up dharma and desire.
Wealth, food, sons, wives and prosperity of others—every greedy man wishes for; all faults arise in the greedy; therefore a king should not take on the greedy.
Even a lowly good man one should urge on in sight; the wise should destroy all the undertakings and aims of his enemies.
A counsellor known among the righteous, guarded, trusted, Pandava, of good family, is sufficient for gathering the kingdom, king.
Hear in brief with your intellect, god among men, these dharmas set forth that proceed by rule; the king who follows and applies them is able to protect the earth.
If happiness is seen born of misconduct and lack of rule, forced and of many kinds, there is no course for such a king; there is no highest happiness born of the realm.

Distinguished by wealth, honoured for intellect and character, endowed with qualities, of valour seen in battle, seen in virtues—the self-possessed king soon, attending to the good, slays his enemies.
He should see the means by various paths of action, and not fix his mind on what is without means; a man who sees faults does not gain superior fortune, vast fame and wealth.
In the course of affection and in turning back, knowing among friends and turning from both, whatever friend bears a heavy burden, the wise man should call that very one most affectionate.
Fix your mind on these duties of kings told by me and on the protection of men; you will easily gain the fruit of merit, for all, best of the world, has dharma as its root."

Of gods, sages, ancestors and great souls, of yakshas, rakshasas and pishachas, and especially of mortals,
mahabharata:12:121.3	of all creatures in the world, even those living among animals, the rod, all-pervading and of great splendour, is the best, lord.
mahabharata:12:121.4	Thus you have said: the whole moving and unmoving is to be ruled by the rod; it is seen attached to the world, with gods, demons and men.
mahabharata:12:121.5	This I wish to know in truth, bull of the Bharatas: what is the rod, of what kind is the rod, what form, what support,
mahabharata:12:121.6	of what nature, how constituted, of how many forms, how lord; how does that rod stay awake over the subjects, with attentive self?
mahabharata:12:121.7	And who stays awake, protecting this before and after? Who is known first, who second, named the rod? In what is the rod established, and what is considered its goal?
[Bhishma said:] "Hear, descendant of Kuru, what the rod is and how it is to be applied; for the rod alone here is that on which everything depends.
Vyavahara is deemed the name of dharma, great king; how could it be lost to one attentive in the worlds? For this reason vyavahara is called vyavahara.
This was said before by Manu long ago, and by Vasishtha, and it is the great utterance of Brahma about birth.
This saying was spoken earlier, hence they call it the earlier saying; and from the telling of vyavahara it is here called vyavahara.
From a rightly applied rod the three aims constantly proceed; the rod is a supreme divinity, in form like a fire with flaming crest.
Dark as a blue lotus petal, four-fanged, four-armed, eight-footed, many-eyed, with ears like pegs and hair standing upright,
matted, two-tongued, copper-faced, clad in the hide of the king of beasts—this fierce form the rod always bears, hard to withstand.
Sword, mace, bow, spear, trident, club, arrow, pestle, axe, discus, lance, staff, javelin and dart,
all weapons that there are in the world—the rod alone, the self of all, moves embodied in the world.
Splitting, cutting, afflicting, severing, tearing, rending, slaying and running upon—the rod itself moves about.
It is the sword, the slayer, dharma, with a sharp path, hard to approach, the womb of fortune, victory, the ruler, vyavahara, the ever-wakeful.
It is scripture, the Brahmana's mantra, the ruler, gone to the earlier saying, guardian of dharma, imperishable, divine, going to truth, ever going, a seizer.
Unattached, Rudra's son, eldest of Manu's line, auspicious doer—these are the names of the rod told, Yudhishthira.
The rod is the blessed Vishnu, sacrifice, Narayana the lord, ever bearing a great form, called the Great Person.
As said, the daughter of Brahma—Lakshmi, Niti, Sarasvati—is Dandaniti, supporter of the world; the rod has many bodies.
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, dharma and adharma, strength and weakness, ill fortune and good fortune, merit and demerit, virtue and vice,
desire and absence of desire, season, month, night, day, moment, displeasure and favour, joy, anger, calm and restraint,
fate and human effort, release and non-release, fear and fearlessness, harm and non-harm, austerity and sacrifice, control, poison and non-poison,
end and beginning and middle, the expansion of deeds, pride, negligence, arrogance, hypocrisy, steadiness, policy and impolicy,
weakness and strength, pride and stiffness, expense and income, humility and release, time and non-time, Bharata,
falsehood, knowledge and ignorance, truth, faith and faithlessness, impotence and resolve, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
sharpness and gentleness, death, coming and non-coming, failure and success, what is to be done and not done, strength and weakness,
envy and freedom from envy, dharma and adharma, shamelessness and shame, modesty, prosperity and calamity,
energy, skill in work, learning, power of speech, true understanding—thus, descendant of Kuru, the rod has many forms in this world.
If the rod did not exist here, they would crush one another; from fear of the rod they do not kill one another, Yudhishthira.
Subjects protected by the rod, king, day by day make the king prosper here; therefore the rod is the refuge.
It quickly establishes this world, lord of men; dharma, established in truth, abides in the Brahmanas.
Twice-born, joined to dharma, are the best and become joined to the Vedas; sacrifice came from the Vedas, and sacrifice pleases the gods.
And the gods, pleased, always yield to Indra; and Shakra gives food, favouring these creatures.
And the breaths of all beings are ever established in food; therefore the subjects are established, and the rod stays awake over them.
Thus, and for this purpose, the rod has become the kshatriya state; protecting the subjects it stays awake, ever well disposed and imperishable.
Lord, person, life-breath, being, wealth, Prajapati, self of beings, soul—it is called by these eight names.
The rod gave him surely sovereignty and might; ever joined in strength with policy, it is of a fivefold nature.
Family, arms, wealth, ministers and wisdom are said to be strengths, and with eightfold goods the other strength is gained, Yudhishthira.
Elephants, horses, chariots, footmen, boats, forced labour, and guides and spies—that is called the eight-limbed strength.
Of the eight-limbed one, joined: elephants and elephant-riders, horsemen and footmen, ministers and suppliers of provisions,
mendicants, judges, astrologers and diviners, treasury, allies, grain and all equipment—
the seven constituents and the eight limbs, which they know as the body here: of the kingdom the rod is a limb, and the rod is also its origin.
By the Lord, with effort, the rod was given to the kshatriya to uphold; the rod is self-same, eternal; there is no other more to be honoured by kings, so showing dharma.

By Brahma, for the protection of the world and the establishment of one's own dharma, vyavahara arose resting on the master's authority and another besides; hence that which is seen united, marked by the master's authority.
Vyavahara has the Veda as its self, and is called resting on the Veda; and, tiger among men, it is rooted in the original and also stated in the scriptures.
And the rod that is told, marked by the master's authority, is not to be known as resting on the king, but as resting on the rod itself.
Even that seen as resting on the rod is held to be of the nature of vyavahara; and vyavahara that is held to be so has the Veda as its sphere.
And what is born of the Veda is dharma, showing virtue; dharma arises resting on dharma, as done by the perfected.
Vyavahara, protector of the subjects, ordained by Brahma, Yudhishthira, supports the three worlds, truth-souled and increasing prosperity.
What is the rod is seen by us as the eternal vyavahara; and the vyavahara that is seen is dharma, as we have heard; what is the Veda is dharma, and what is dharma is the good path.
Brahma Prajapati was first, then the grandfather, of all the worlds, of gods, demons and rakshasas, of men and serpents, and he is the maker of beings.
Therefore this vyavahara of ours is marked by the master's authority; hence we have spoken this illustration of vyavahara.
Mother, father, brother, wife and household priest—for kings there is none not to be punished who does not stand in his own dharma."
That king, ever devoted to dharma, the great ascetic, with his wife went to Munjaprishtha, honoured by hosts of divine sages.
There, on the peak of the Himalaya, on Meru, the golden mountain, where at the munja fig-tree Rama directed the removal of matted locks,
since then, king of kings, that place, resorted to by Rudra, has been called Munjaprishtha by sages of strict vows.
There, joined with many qualities consisting of sacred learning, approved by the Brahmanas, he became like a divine sage.
Once Mandhata, a king, friend of Shakra and honoured by him, scourge of foes, of unabashed spirit, came to him.
Having approached King Vasuhoma, Mandhata, seeing him eminent by austerity, stood up with humility.
Vasuhoma too offered the king a cow and water of welcome and asked after the welfare of his eight-limbed kingdom.
He asked, as it was done by the good in the past, one who followed him rightly: "What shall I do for you, king?"
He was born as Kshupa, Prajapati, scourge of foes; he was then the officiating priest, king, at the sacrifice of that great soul.
When Brahma's sacrifice was under way, best of kings, the rod, being engaged in glad conduct, disappeared.
When it had vanished, confusion arose among the subjects; there was no what-to-do or not-to-do, nor edible and inedible.
Drinkable and undrinkable, where was success? They harmed one another; no thing was fit or unfit to approach; others' property and one's own were equal.
They plundered one another like dogs a piece of meat; the strong slew the weak; it became lawless.
Then the Grandfather, having honoured the blessed eternal Vishnu, the boon-giving god Mahadeva, said:
Here you ought to show, rightly, compassion alone; let it be so arranged that there be no confusion here.
Then the blessed one, bearing trident and matted hair, best of gods, reflected long and from himself created the rod by himself.
From it he created Dandaniti, the divine Sarasvati, who follows dharma and policy, renowned in the three worlds.
Again the blessed one, wielding the best of tridents, reflected long and made a lord for each of those groups.
He made the god of a thousand eyes lord of the gods, and made Yama Vaivasvata lord of the ancestors.
He made Kubera lord of riches and rakshasas, Meru lord of mountains, and the great ocean lord of rivers.
He appointed Varuna lord in the dominion of the waters and of the gods, Death lord of life-breaths, and Fire lord of lights.
The lord made the great-souled, eternal, large-eyed Mahadeva guardian of the Rudras.
He made Vasishtha lord of Brahmanas, Jatavedas of the Vasus, the sun of the lights, and the moon of the stars.
He made Amshumant lord of plants, and ordained Kumara Skanda, twelve-armed, best lord of beings, as king.
He made Time the lord of all, whose nature is restraint in dissolution, of death, of the fourfold division, of pain and of pleasure.
The Lord of all bodies, king of kings, lord of wealth, is, according to scripture, the trident-handed among all the Rudras.
To that one, the son born of Brahma, Kshupa, he gave the rod, best lord of subjects, even among all upholders of dharma.
Then Mahadeva, when the sacrifice had been completed according to rule, gave the rod, the guardian of dharma, honoured to Vishnu.
Vishnu gave it to Angiras; Angiras, the best of sages, gave it to Indra and Marichi; Marichi gave it to Bhrigu.
Bhrigu gave that rod, conjoined with dharma, to the sages; the sages to the guardians of the world; and the guardians of the world to Kshupa.
Kshupa gave it to Manu, son of the Aditya; Shraddhadeva Manu, son of the sun, gave it to his sons for the sake of subtle dharma and wealth, as one who protects.
The rod must be applied by division, by dharma and not at will: harsh words, restraint, binding, and fines are outer acts.
Mutilation of the body or death should not be for a small cause; various bodily torments, giving up the body and banishment are in order.
In order the rod stays awake protecting the subjects: Indra the blessed stays awake, and from Indra Agni Vibhavasu.
From Agni Varuna stays awake, from Varuna Prajapati, and from Prajapati dharma, whose nature is discipline.
From dharma, Brahma's son, the eternal resolve; and from resolve energy stays awake, protecting.
From that energy the herbs, from the herbs the mountains, and from the mountains sap stays awake by the quality of sap.
The goddess Nirriti stays awake, and the lights from Nirriti; the Vedas are founded on the lights, and then the lord Hayashiras.
From him Brahma the Grandfather, the lord, imperishable, stays awake; and from the Grandfather Mahadeva, the blessed Shiva.
The Vishvadevas from Shiva, and from the Vishvadevas the sages, from the sages the blessed Soma, and from Soma the eternal gods.
Know that from the gods the Brahmanas stay awake in the world; from the Brahmanas the kshatriyas protect the worlds by dharma, and from the kshatriyas the eternal fixed and moving.
The subjects stay awake in this world, and the rod stays awake in them; the rod, the summing up of all, is a lord like the Grandfather.
Time stays awake in the beginning, middle and end, Bharata; the lord of all the world is Mahadeva, Prajapati.
God of gods, Shiva, Sharva, the lord stays ever awake—Kapardin, Shankara, Rudra, Bhava, Sthanu, husband of Uma.
Thus this rod is renowned in beginning, middle and end; a protector of the earth who knows dharma should act by it as justice requires."
[Bhishma said:] "A man who hears this opinion of Vasuhoma and, having heard, acts rightly, a king, will attain his desires.
Thus I have told you all about the rod, bull among men, the restrainer of all the world, when it is overcome by dharma, Bharata."
What are the roots of dharma, wealth and desire, and what is the origin of the three? They are connected with one another and also proceed separately.
[Bhishma said:] "When they are well disposed toward the determination of the world's order, the three are fixed in the stations born of time.
The body is rooted in dharma, wealth is desire's fruit, they say; all of them are rooted in intention, and intention is of the nature of the objects of sense.
And the objects, in sum, are for the accomplishment of food; this is the root of the three aims; renunciation is called liberation.
Dharma is the guarding of the body; wealth is wished for dharma's sake; desire here has pleasure as its fruit; all these are of the quality of passion.
One should practise these near, without abandoning them in mind, free of darkness, regarding dharma and the rest as the end of desire.
The best intellect of the three aims is what one may attain in an instant; one should know by intellect in this matter, not by a low day.
The stain of dharma is ill-thinking, the stain of wealth concealment, the stain of desire excessive delight, again turned by one's own qualities."
Having saluted the seated sage Kamanda, the king Angarishtha asked, after making a pact to take turns:

The king who commits sin, made so by the force of desire and delusion, when death is near for him, sage, what would be the destruction of that sin?
mahabharata:12:123.13	One who here out of ignorance practises adharma as dharma, and that widely known in the world—how should a king turn him back?
[Kamanda said:] "One who gives up dharma and wealth and follows desire alone, by abandoning dharma and wealth, comes here to the destruction of wisdom.
Delusion destroys wisdom and destroys dharma and wealth; from it come unbelief and misconduct.
When a king does not restrain the greatly corrupt who misbehave, the world is alarmed at him as at a snake that has entered the house.
The subjects do not follow him, nor Brahmanas nor the good; thence he meets ruin and comes to be fit to be slain.
Cast down and despised, he lives a life of misery; and if he lives cast down, that may be a pure death.
On this the teachers say, for the removal of sin: the threefold knowledge should be served and honour paid to Brahmanas.
He should be great-minded in dharma and marry into a great family, and serve the forbearing and high-minded Brahmanas.
He should mutter prayers, be given to water rites, of pleasant face, fixed on nothing else; having put the evildoers outside, he should enter among the righteous.
He should win them over with sweet speech and by deed; saying always "I am as I am", he should proclaim the virtues of others.
Thus, free of sin, one of such conduct soon becomes greatly esteemed, and quells even hard sins; there is no doubt in this.
Whatever the teachers say is the highest dharma, do that so; by the favour of the teachers you will attain the highest good."

If that can be known by us, best of upholders of dharma, I wish to hear all of it as it is understood.
mahabharata:12:124.3	How is good conduct attained? I wish to hear, Bharata; what is its mark? Tell me, best of speakers.
[Bhishma said:] "Long ago Duryodhana, tormented at seeing prosperity come to you, told Dhritarashtra, giver of honour,
at Indraprastha, great king, about the mockery in the hall of you and your brothers; hear all that, Bharata.
Having seen your hall and your supreme prosperity, Duryodhana, then seated, told it all to his father.
Hearing Duryodhana's words, Dhritarashtra then said this to Duryodhana together with Karna:

Why are you tormented, son? I wish to hear it truly; having heard, I shall console you if you will be rightly set.
mahabharata:12:124.9	You have attained great sovereignty, scourge of enemies; your brothers are all servants, and friends and relatives likewise.
[Dhritarashtra said:] "If you desire, dear son, the fortune that Yudhishthira has, or an even better one, tiger among men, become of good conduct, my son.
By good conduct the three worlds can be conquered, without doubt; nothing is unattainable in the world for those of good conduct.
Mandhata in one night, Janamejaya in three days, Nabhaga in seven nights obtained the earth.
All those kings were of good conduct and self-control; therefore the earth, bought by their qualities, came to them of itself.
On this too they recite this ancient history, told long ago by Narada, relying on good conduct, Bharata.
The kingdom of the great-souled Mahendra was seized by Prahlada, and by relying on good conduct the Daitya brought the three worlds under his power.
Then Shakra stood before Brihaspati with joined palms, and the greatly wise one said, "I wish to know the highest good."
Then the blessed Brihaspati told the highest knowledge of the final good to the lord of gods, descendant of Kuru.
This much is the good, said Brihaspati; but Indra asked again, "Where might there be something more?"
[Brihaspati said:] "There is something greater, dear one, with the great-souled Bhargava; seek it there, good luck to you, Purandara, once more."
[Dhritarashtra said:] "Then from Bhargava of great fame he obtained knowledge of his own good, and with affection, once more, the supremely radiant one.
Permitted by the great-souled Bhargava too, Shatakratu said again to Shukra, "There is a good yet more."
Bhargava, knower of dharma, said, "There is a special knowledge with the great-souled Prahlada," and he was glad.
Then Paka's chastiser, becoming a Brahmana, went to Prahlada and the wise one said, "I wish to know the highest good."
But Prahlada said to the Brahmana, "There is no leisure, best of the twice-born, for one attached to rule over the three worlds; so I cannot instruct you."
The Brahmana said, "At what time would there be leisure? Then I wish to be instructed in whatever may be the matter at hand."
Then King Prahlada was pleased with the Vedic speaker, and saying "So be it," at an auspicious time gave him the truth of knowledge.
The Brahmana too, according to rule, performed the highest service to his teacher with every feeling, as he wished in mind.
And he asked him many times, "Scourge of foes, knower of dharma, how did you obtain rule over the three worlds? Tell me the reason."
[Prahlada said:] "I am not envious, best of twice-born, nor ever think 'I am king'; I restrain and carry the words of the speakers of offerings to the ancestors, dear one."
Neither Time nor the serpent nor Death is the cause here; by his own deeds this child has gone to death by time.
His son Karandhama was born at the beginning of the Treta age, glorious, not inferior to Indra, hard to conquer even by the gods.
My hundred sons, brave and never fleeing in battle, were slain; I do not grieve for that, for they know that as kshatriya dharma. Having said this, the Kaurava addressed the king of dharma.
I go now to the path, and I swear by truth, for those who were slain in sleep by that evil-souled one.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Ignoble deed by a noble one, thousand-eyed, is hard to do, noble one; let me not be joined with that fortune for whose sake I would abandon a devoted person."
Thus King Yudhishthira reflected in many ways, overcome with grief and sorrow, his senses disturbed with anxious thought.
